analysis.one_liner: Would have let the regional Bell phone companies enter long-distance service after one year, automatically.
analysis.headline: The bill was never voted on: it drew zero cosponsors, got one subcommittee hearing, and died in the Senate Commerce Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 1996 telecommunications law, the regional Bell companies could only sell long-distance service after federal regulators confirmed they had opened their local phone markets to competitors. This bill would have thrown that requirement out: one year after passage, the Bells could sell long-distance and local service nationwide, and no state or local law could stop them. It was introduced by Senator McCain, referred to the Commerce Committee, received a single subcommittee hearing, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: The Bell operating companies — the huge regional phone companies carved out of AT&T, such as SBC, Bell Atlantic, BellSouth, Ameritech and US West — would have gained the most, getting automatic entry into the interstate and intrastate long-distance market without having to prove they had opened their local monopolies to rivals [S2][S3]. The bill's findings argued that removing these restraints would lower prices, create jobs, and extend advanced services to rural areas [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It gives Bell operating companies and their affiliates a firm legal right to provide interstate and intrastate telecommunications services one year after enactment, overriding any prerequisite in the Communications Act that would otherwise condition their entry on opening local markets [S3].
It supersedes any state or local law that would prevent the Bells from providing those services, removing state-level regulatory barriers [S2][S3].

The bill's findings state that open competition would benefit prices, availability, quality, and job creation, and that rural areas would benefit from advanced services once restrictions were lifted [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Long-distance carriers like AT&T, MCI and Sprint would face the Bells entering their markets with a built-in advantage: the Bells would still dominate local service because the bill deemed the market-opening prerequisites met without verification. Competitive local phone companies would lose their main lever — the 1996 Act's checklist that forced the Bells to open local networks before entering long distance. Consumers could pay through less local competition if that leverage disappeared.

drawbacks.text: The bill deems every market-opening prerequisite under the Communications Act satisfied on a fixed date, with no verification by the FCC or state regulators that the Bells had actually opened their local monopolies to competitors [S3] — eliminating the central enforcement mechanism of the 1996 Act's bargain.
It preempts state and local law, stripping states of their traditional authority over intrastate phone service [S2][S3].

Supporters would have to concede that handing the Bells long-distance entry while their local monopolies remained intact could entrench those incumbents rather than increase competition, contrary to the bill's own competition findings [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill promised faster competition and lower prices, but its design undercut that promise: it removed the one requirement — verified opening of local markets — that was supposed to make Bell competition real, and replaced it with an automatic start date. Whether consumers would have gained depended entirely on the Bells voluntarily opening their networks once the lever forcing them to do so was gone. As drafted, the main certain winner was the Bell companies themselves.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the Senate Commerce Committee, got a single subcommittee hearing, and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator McCain introduced the bill on March 16, 1998, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
On March 25, 1998, the Subcommittee on Communications held a hearing — the only committee action the bill ever received [S5].
The committee never reported the bill and the Senate never voted on it; the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill died [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Bell companies did not get their automatic long-distance entry, so long-distance carriers like AT&T and MCI and the competitive local phone companies kept the 1996 Act's market-opening protections. Consumers kept the legal requirement that the Bells prove local competition before expansion — though the Bells also kept their dominant local position a little longer.

for.name: John McCain
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-AZ), sponsor and chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; as committee chair, held a subcommittee hearing but never brought the bill to a markup or the floor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred and the bill had zero cosponsors, so the fight never took a partisan shape; the record shows only one sponsor and no recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Regional Bell operating companies (SBC, Bell Atlantic, BellSouth, Ameritech, US West)
industries.note: The bill would have given them automatic entry into the interstate and intrastate long-distance market within a year, while deeming every market-opening prerequisite already met — so they could expand without opening their local monopolies to rivals. Ordinary consumers would depend entirely on those incumbents choosing to compete against themselves.

The Bells entering long distance without having opened local markets would put new, locally-entrenched competition into the carriers' core business. Their interest ran with consumers who wanted genuinely open local markets first.

industries.industry: Competitive local exchange carriers (new local phone companies)
industries.note: The 1996 Act's prerequisites were these companies' main legal lever to force the Bells to share local networks; declaring them automatically met would remove that leverage, making it harder for smaller competitors to break into local phone service.
The bill supersedes any state or local law blocking Bell services and shifts oversight of intrastate service to the states only in name, preempting state authority over phone markets.
